finding.headline: For 2027, the 401(k) limit rises to $25,500, and the IRA limit stays at $7,500.
details: The 401(k) limit for 2027 is $25,500, up from $24,500 for 2026. The IRA limit remains $7,500 for 2027.
You are 40 and plan to retire at 65, so you have 25 years to save. Use the 401(k) and IRA limits above as the yearly ceiling for each of you.
At 65, Social Security benefits stop growing once you reach age 70. Sign up for Medicare at 65 so that your coverage does not get delayed or cost more.

finding.headline: The spending goal of $85,000 a year lasts in only 9 of 100 scenarios; the basics are paid in 90 of 100.
details: The plan kept is a simple plan: stocks at 110 minus your age, with Social Security claimed at age 68. The most the household can spend and still be safe in 90 of 100 scenarios is $43,900 a year, about $3,658 a month. That is about 52% of the $85,000 goal.

The goal runs out in 91 of 100 scenarios, so the plan does not cover the full goal. Median savings at retirement are $592,000, but the median at age 96 is $0. Markets are uncertain, and these results can change.
The gap is $41,100 a year. Closing it needs more saving, a lower spending goal, or a later retirement, and a planner can help you test those choices.

finding.headline: You can count on $43,900 a year, about your basics.
details: Your basics cost about $43,800 a year.
Your spending goal of $85,000 a year lasts in 9 of 100 scenarios.

assumptions: All figures are in today's dollars: what money buys now, not the larger sums prices will reach.

Savings grow on average 5.0% a year above inflation in stocks and 1.8% in bonds, with good and bad years. The plan tests many possible market paths. These are planning figures, not a forecast. They are fixed, so every plan is tested on the same markets; to see a bad stretch, try a What If such as markets fall 30%.

Until you retire you save about $6,056 a year: $2,400 into a 401(k) or IRA, $3,656 of take-home pay left after your spending, which the plan assumes you save. If that is wrong, change 'Yearly saving' in your answers.
Pay stays at today's level until you retire, with no raises. This is fixed: raises are not certain, so the plan does not count on them. If your pay changes, change it in your answers.
Social Security uses the figure you gave, read as the benefit at 67. Your answers show $38,600 a year from 67. This plan starts it at 68 for each of you, which pays about $41,700 a year.
A partner with little pay of their own gets half of the other's benefit at 67, less if started sooner.
After the first death (at the shorter life expectancy), Social Security falls to the larger of your two benefits, about $21,400 a year, and spending falls to 75% of what the two of you spend.
If you retire before Medicare starts at 65, health cover costs about $10,000 a person a year until then (an assumption). Other health costs follow CMS figures by age.

Tax uses the 2027 federal brackets, the standard deduction and your state's rates. While you work, 401(k) saving comes off taxable pay. In retirement the plan counts 85% of Social Security as taxable, the most the law allows, so the tax may be a little high.
The plan runs to age 96. There is about a 1 in 4 chance that one of you will live that long (US life table, SOA 2024). People with more money tend to live longer than that table says.
